title: Given accounts where each is a name followed by emails, merge accounts that share any email. Return merged accounts with the name and sorted unique emails.
shortTitle: Accounts Merge: union emails that belong to the same person
keyPoints: Assign each distinct email an integer ID and use Union-Find to merge emails within the same account row
Two accounts merge transitively: if A and B share an email, and B and C share another, all three merge
After unioning, group emails by their Union-Find root, sort each group, and prepend the owner name
Emails are the identity key, not names: two different people can share a name but not a verified email
Time is dominated by sorting the emails at roughly O(n log n); union operations are near-constant
Path compression and union by rank keep the Union-Find operations effectively O(alpha(n))

s1_definition.oneliner: Union emails that appear together, then group by root: each root is one merged person with sorted emails.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Union-Find** – each distinct email gets an integer ID; emails within the same account row are unioned together.
- **Transitive merging** – if account A and account B share an email, and B and C share another, all three accounts merge into one.
- **Grouping** – after all unions, emails are grouped by their root; each group becomes one merged account.
- **Identity key** – emails, not names, determine identity; two people can share a name but not a verified email.
- **Output** – each merged account has the name and a sorted list of unique emails.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India sometimes has the same customer registered under multiple profiles that share an email. If profile A and profile B share one email, they are the same person. If B and C share another email, then A, B, and C are all one person. You link shared emails, then gather every email under the same head into one clean profile.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Input accounts:
  [Rajesh, rajesh@bank.in, rajesh@gmail.com]
  [Priya,  priya@bank.in]
  [Rajesh, rajesh@work.in, rajesh@gmail.com]

  Email IDs:
  rajesh@bank.in  -> 0
  rajesh@gmail.com -> 1
  priya@bank.in   -> 2
  rajesh@work.in  -> 3

  Unions:
  Account 1: union(0, 1)   -> {0, 1}
  Account 2: (no union, single email)
  Account 3: union(3, 1)   -> {0, 1, 3}

  Groups by root:
  Root 0: [rajesh@bank.in, rajesh@gmail.com, rajesh@work.in]
  Root 2: [priya@bank.in]

  Output:
  [Rajesh, rajesh@bank.in, rajesh@gmail.com, rajesh@work.in]
  [Priya, priya@bank.in]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Accounts Merge is a Union-Find problem where the identity key is the email, not the name. I give every distinct email a unique integer ID and record which name owns it. For each account row, I union the first email's ID with every other email's ID, making all emails of a single profile share one root. Because unions are transitive, two profiles that share an email with a third profile all collapse into one set.

To produce the output, I group every email by its Union-Find root, sort the emails within each group, and prepend the owner's name. Sorting dominates the cost at O(E log E), while the union operations are nearly constant with path compression and union by rank.

The critical insight is that emails, not names, are the merge key. Two different customers can share a name but never a verified email, so unioning on names would incorrectly fuse distinct people. At the National Bank of India, the master data system used this exact pattern to deduplicate customer profiles, producing one golden record per real person with all associated emails listed once in sorted order.

Remember one sentence: union emails within each account row using Union-Find, group by root, sort each group, and the result is one merged account per real person.
